defects.description: Separate user pools establish identity separation, not authorization for individual API operations. The design must specify adjuster-only authorization for decision endpoints and claim-ownership checks for customer reads, uploads and downloads.

End-to-end recovery still has dual-write gaps: a failure between creating the DynamoDB record and starting the workflow can strand a claim, while SES acceptance followed by failure before writing the notification flag can produce duplicate email. Execution names and a sent flag do not resolve these boundaries; submission reconciliation and ambiguous-delivery handling are needed.
Make upload finalization explicit: start automated checks only after the required objects exist and their references have been committed, rather than merely after issuing upload URLs.

Explicitly select Standard workflows and define complete step-level logging, audit retention and lifecycle policies. Native completed-execution history does not provide the assumed seven-year audit retention.

reviews.summary: A strong serverless workflow foundation covers the human wait and operational failure visibility, but authorization and cross-service recovery need hardening.

defects.description: CloudTrail is incorrectly characterized as providing an immutable, compliance-grade log intrinsically. Neither CloudTrail nor its CloudWatch destination makes the stored evidence immutable; no protected archive or integrity-validation configuration is specified, leaving the stated audit protection unsafe to rely on.

The explanation conflates the one-year maximum Standard workflow execution duration with audit-history retention. Completed Standard execution history is retained for 90 days, so longer audit requirements must be met through separately retained application records or logs.
The CloudTrail-to-CloudWatch integration omits a configured trail and its S3 delivery destination. CloudWatch forwarding supplements a trail rather than replacing its S3 log destination.

Idempotency is described only for automated checks. Intake, workflow starts, decision callbacks and notification delivery need explicit duplicate handling and recovery across DynamoDB, Step Functions and SES; workflow retries alone do not make these side effects safe.

HTTP API JWT authorization does not automatically enforce Cognito group membership. The adjuster function's explicit role check is therefore important; describe group authorization as application logic rather than a built-in JWT-authorizer check.
Specify a completed-upload submission boundary before starting checks, including handling missing, incomplete or replaced documents.

reviews.summary: The callback workflow and application audit records are sensible, but false audit guarantees, incorrect history retention and incomplete recovery handling materially weaken the design.

defects.description: Private workers have no specified NAT or VPC-endpoint egress path. Image pulls and access to services such as STS, CloudWatch and X-Ray require an explicit reachable path; the HTTPS arrows do not establish that networking.

No AWS Load Balancer Controller or equivalent Ingress and target-registration mechanism is specified. The ALB-to-worker arrows alone do not connect the existing Helm-managed Services and Ingress resources to working ALB targets.

Specify database credential delivery, TLS for MySQL connections and security-group restrictions between the ALB, workloads and data services; private subnet placement and IRSA do not define these controls.

Tracing needs existing or newly configured application instrumentation and cross-service context propagation. An OpenTelemetry collector forwards spans but does not create complete distributed traces by itself.
Name the HPA metrics source and node-capacity autoscaler, and define resource requests and minimum multi-AZ capacity to implement the stated scaling assumption.

reviews.summary: Managed-node EKS is a good fit for minimal-change Helm migration, with the main gaps being private-service connectivity, ingress integration and operational configuration.

defects.description: Fargate is selected without checking the existing charts against its Kubernetes restrictions. DaemonSets, privileged containers, host networking and some storage patterns are unsupported, so unchanged manifests cannot be promised without a compatibility assessment and an EC2-node fallback.

Specify the Fargate-compatible observability deployment: built-in Fluent Bit log routing and an appropriate metrics and OpenTelemetry pipeline. A generic reference to Container Insights leaves the required configuration unclear.
Document application tracing instrumentation and context propagation, preferably reusing existing instrumentation or compatible auto-instrumentation to preserve the minimal-change goal.
TLS is shown for ingress and data-service connections, but service-to-service TLS between the microservices is not specified despite the design's broader internal-TLS requirement.
Define pod resource requests, replica placement and scaling behavior so that the two-AZ layout provides actual workload resilience rather than merely two available scheduling locations.

reviews.summary: The networking, secrets and security topology is well developed, but Fargate compatibility and its observability setup must be validated before claiming a minimal-change migration.

defects.description: The archive rationale incorrectly presents S3 versioning and KMS encryption as establishing tamper-evidence. Neither supplies CloudTrail digest-based integrity validation, and versioning alone does not protect all versions from privileged deletion; the claimed audit-integrity guarantee is unsafe without additional controls.

The customer-controlled-key requirement is only partially implemented. Explicit settings cover RDS and the archive bucket, but not CloudWatch logs, secrets, registry images or Fargate ephemeral application storage; Fargate storage requires explicit customer-managed-key configuration rather than relying on its default encryption.

The claimed AZ-failure tolerance is not implemented by the shown placements: tasks and NAT appear only in AZ A, and the ALB's required second-AZ subnet configuration is not stated. Deploy tasks across both private subnets and explicitly configure resilient ingress and egress.

Make the administrative-audit scope explicit: a multi-Region trail covering read and write management events, including global-service activity, with defined retention and monitoring for trail changes.
The Route 53 lookup edge should normally be labeled DNS rather than HTTPS; ordinary authoritative DNS resolution is not an HTTPS invocation.

reviews.summary: The design provides suitable container, MFA and TLS building blocks, but overstates audit integrity and leaves customer-key coverage and AZ resilience incomplete.

defects.description: Customer-managed encryption is described for S3, Aurora, secrets and logs, but not the container registry or Fargate ephemeral application storage. Explicitly cover these stores as well; Fargate's default ephemeral-storage encryption does not use a bank-controlled key.

Separate the regional TLS resources from edge resources: the CloudFront ACM certificate must be in us-east-1, the ALB certificate must be in the ALB Region, and the CloudFront WAF ACL needs CLOUDFRONT scope.

Specify that the administrative trail covers all AWS Regions, read and write management events and global-service activity. A single-Region application does not limit the scope of account administration.

Document how the ALB restriction is bound to this CloudFront distribution, such as origin-header verification alongside network restrictions; permitting CloudFront-originated traffic generally is not sufficient to exclude other distributions.

reviews.summary: This is a strong layered-security and multi-AZ design with protected audit storage, needing broader customer-key coverage and a few explicit edge and account-wide configurations.

preference.why: A provides stronger explicit idempotency measures, failure routing and validated audit storage, whereas B makes unsafe audit claims and misstates execution-history retention.
A better preserves existing Kubernetes and Helm workloads through managed EC2 nodes without Fargate compatibility restrictions, although B has more complete networking and secret handling.

B more completely implements layered protection, multi-AZ deployment, least privilege and protected audit retention; A overstates audit integrity and leaves more security and availability controls unspecified.
